alternativeText.text: A young man hands a boy a silver seashell.

elements.text: When he was younger, John loved going to the beach. It meant a whole week to play with his two older brothers, Harry and Trent. But then Harry went away to college, and now Trent had to stay behind for his summer job. John was going to be the only kid at his family's beach house. He pictured himself floating in the water all by himself and sighed.

Before John and his parents left for the beach, Trent pulled John aside. He handed John a sparkly silver seashell. "Harry gave this to me the summer I was ten. Now that you're ten, it's your turn," Trent explained. "When you get to the beach, dip this seashell into the ocean."
"What will happen?" John asked.
"You'll see," Trent said with a wink.

He held the seashell with both hands, closed his eyes, and took a deep breath. Then he pictured his family's beach house.

When John opened his eyes again, he was splashing in the water near the shore. His dad was still sleeping on the sand, and his mom was still calmly reading her book. It looked like no time had passed. He smiled. His parents didn't seem distressed that he had disappeared.

elements.text: "Wowza! What an amazing machine!" Gabloon said to himself. He thought of how great life would be if he had a machine like that.

Gabloon lived alone and had no friends to talk to, so he spent hours standing at his window, watching the fairy family use their new machine. He noticed that they never used the machine to make anything fancy. They just used their machine to make simple things like plain shoes, warm blankets, or fresh vegetables. Surely the machine could make much more than that! In fact, it seemed like the magic machine was wasted on the fairy family.

Being a clever and somewhat sneaky little goblin, Gabloon began to form a plan. From his piggy bank, he took out a gold coin. Then, as he waited for the fairy family to fall asleep, he played with the coin, smiling to himself.

elements.text: People sometimes expected Sima and Rohan to act the same because they were twins. And it was true that they both loved reading. But the minute they walked into any bookstore, Sima and Rohan went in different directions. Sima wanted stories about magical creatures, while Rohan found books that explained how trains work.
This time, Sima tugged her brother's arm before they parted ways. "You should come with me. Life's more fun with magic in it."
"I'm not interested in magical stories," Rohan said. "It's all fake."
Sima pointed at a winged creature flying near a lamp. "Then why is there a fairy over there?"
Rohan laughed. "That's just a moth," he said. "I'm going to find a book with something real in it. See you later." He walked off.
"So what if that fairy was only a moth?" Sima muttered. "It looked like a fairy, and that's what made it fun."
